sections.overview: The Black-headed Gull breeds widely across Europe and northern Asia, with a small population on Canada’s east coast. Many birds from colder regions migrate south or west for winter, while populations in mild areas may remain.
sections.identification: Adults are about 34–39 cm long, span 100–110 cm and usually weigh 166–400 g; males average heavier, though sexes overlap. The breeding hood is chocolate brown, not black; in winter the head is white with a dark spot behind each eye, and the red bill and legs, black wingtips and white wing edge remain useful marks.
sections.habitat: It breeds and feeds on coastal and inland wetlands, including marshes, reedbeds, lakes, ponds and estuaries. Gravel pits, reservoirs, settling ponds, fields and towns also host birds.
sections.diet: This flexible omnivore eats aquatic and terrestrial insects, earthworms and other invertebrates, as well as fish, rodents, seeds, grain, berries and discarded food. In fields it may stamp the ground with webbed feet to bring worms to the surface. At water margins it takes prey from the surface or dips its head below.
sections.behavior: During breeding, adults mob birds that threaten eggs or chicks, but dense flocks may flee falcons attacking adults.
sections.reproduction: In spring, pairs form through visual displays and calls; courtship includes the male regurgitating food for the female before mating. The pair then defends a small territory within its colony. Both adults build a shallow nest from vegetation, twigs and other plant matter, usually in a marsh, reedbed or island, and sometimes on an artificial raft. A usual clutch contains two or three eggs, incubated by both adults for about 23–26 days. The downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching but depend on their parents, which guard and feed them by regurgitating food onto the ground for the brood. Young usually fledge at 34–36 days and reach breeding maturity around two years.
sections.ecology: In Dutch colonies, gulls sometimes defend Sandwich Tern nests from predators, yet also steal tern fish and eat their eggs and chicks.
sections.conservation: The global assessment is Least Concern, although regional trends differ. British coastal breeding populations declined between the 1998–2002 and 2015–2021 censuses, with several pressures involved; avian influenza subsequently caused further mortality in 2022–2023.

sources.title: Seabird Population Trends and Causes of Change: 1986–2024 — BTO Research Report 795 (2026)
